text:
Kirill Kaprizov took his first shot of the night 21 seconds into overtime, and that was enough. His power-play slap shot, set up by Matt Boldy and Quinn Hughes, gave Minnesota a 2-1 win in Montreal that the Canadiens will spend a couple of days being angry about. Eric Engels of Sportsnet summed up the local mood as "a great game ruined by terrible officiating." Our numbers say Montreal deserved this one 62% of the time. The reason they didn't get it is Jesper Wallstedt.

Wallstedt made 27 saves and stopped 2.6 goals more than the shots deserved. His best moment came in the second period on Alexandre Texier, a 30% chance, and Montreal's two power plays produced 1.02 expected goals (the quality of chances) without a goal. Michael Russo of The Athletic said the night drew a Carey Price comparison. The Wild's notes have Wallstedt at 12-2-3, leading the league in wins and saves. That's a goalie carrying a team, and it's worth noticing how much of Minnesota's season rides on him.

The goals came late. Bobby Brink, who had five shots and was Minnesota's most dangerous forward, scored on a snap shot 2:53 into the third. Minnesota is 11-0-4 when it scores first, and for most of the period that record looked safe. Then Nick Suzuki tied it with the goalie pulled at 18:22, off Cole Caufield and Lane Hutson, a goal that lifted Montreal's win chance from 11% to 52%. Hutson played 26:48 and was on the ice for 2.06 expected goals for.

The overtime power play swung it back. Caufield ended regulation in the penalty box, and Minnesota needed about 20 seconds of the advantage. Jacob Fowler was good for Montreal too, 22 saves and 0.9 goals better than expected, which made it a goaltenders' night at both ends.

It was the Wild's first overtime win of the season. Montreal gets a point and a grievance. The bigger concern for the Canadiens is that this kind of game, plenty of chances and one goal, keeps happening.
headline: Wallstedt steals one, Kaprizov needs one shot
